modifyDefinitions.Purely actual actualizer (Unmoved Mover): The conclusion of Stage 1 of the Aristotelian proof: something that actualizes potentials without itself having any potential that needs actualizing. It is also called pure actuality or pure act (actus purus), and is described as “unmoved” or “unactualized” because nothing in it needs to be made actual.
modifyDefinitions.Probabilistic / abductive argument: An argument that concludes a hypothesis is the most probable, simplest, or best-fitting explanation of some evidence, while allowing that some alternative could in principle be correct. Inductive arguments (generalizing from observed cases) and abductive arguments (inferring to the best explanation) are of this kind, and are judged by criteria like parsimony and fit with background theory.

newTerms.definition: In Feser's sense, the cause at the head of a hierarchical series: “first” because it has causal power in an underived way, not because it came earliest in time. An uncaused cause is one that not only lacks a cause but could not have one, because it lacks what makes other things need causes.
newTerms.example: In the cup–desk–floor series, the first cause is whatever holds things up without having to be held up itself.
newTerms.origin: Traditional phrase from Aristotle and the Scholastics (Aquinas' Second Way argues to a first uncaused cause).
newTerms.confuseWith: The earliest event in time, such as the Big Bang: the first cause in these proofs is compatible with a universe that had no beginning.

newTerms.definition: The attribute of being one and unique: there not only is but could be only one God. Feser argues it follows because nothing purely actual, absolutely simple, or subsistent existence itself could be differentiated from another of its kind. Monotheism is belief in one such God.
newTerms.example: Two purely actual beings would need some feature one has and the other lacks, but nothing purely actual lacks anything.
newTerms.origin: Greek monos, “alone,” plus theos, “god”; the attribute of unity is treated at length in Aquinas and in chapter 6.
newTerms.confuseWith: Mere numerical singleness as a matter of fact: classical theism holds that more than one God is impossible in principle, not just absent.

newTerms.definition: Being immaterial means not being made of matter; being incorporeal means having no body. God has both attributes, since whatever is material is changeable and exists in time, while God is immutable and eternal.
newTerms.example: Unlike a statue of Zeus or a body of any kind, the purely actual cause has no physical parts or location.
newTerms.origin: Latin in-, “not,” plus materia, “matter,” and corpus, “body.”
newTerms.confuseWith: Being made of some exotic, invisible stuff (like a ghost or energy field): immaterial means not material at all.

newTerms.definition: Omnipotence is all-powerfulness; an omnipotent being can do anything that is possible to do. Feser argues that the purely actual cause is omnipotent because power is the ability to actualize potentials and this cause is the source of all actualizing power whatsoever.
newTerms.example: Every power any creature has — the sun's to melt ice, your hand's to move a stick — is derived from and sustained by the first cause.
newTerms.origin: Latin omnis, “all,” plus potens, “powerful.”
newTerms.confuseWith: Being able to do logically impossible things (like making a round square): omnipotence concerns what is possible, not contradictions.

newTerms.definition: Omniscience is all-knowingness; an omniscient being knows everything there is to know. In Feser's proofs, God's knowledge follows from his being the cause of all things together with the principle of proportionate causality, and from the Augustinian argument that all universals and truths exist in the divine intellect.
newTerms.example: Since every possibility and every truth exists as an idea in the divine intellect, nothing knowable is unknown to God.
newTerms.origin: Latin omnis, “all,” plus scientia, “knowledge.”
newTerms.confuseWith: Knowing things by observing them as we do: classical theism holds that God knows things by knowing himself as their cause, not by gathering information.

newTerms.definition: A thing is perfect to the extent it has actualized the potentials proper to its nature and lacks privations; it is good to the extent it realizes what it is. A purely actual being has no unrealized potential and no privation, so it is perfect and perfectly good.
newTerms.example: A good painter has realized his potential for craftsmanship; a squirrel hit by a car suffers a privation. God has neither gaps nor defects.
newTerms.origin: Latin perfectus, “completed” or “thoroughly made”; the analysis of goodness as actualization is Aristotelian and Thomistic.
newTerms.confuseWith: Moral goodness in the sense of obeying duties: divine goodness is first of all metaphysical completeness, from which goodness in every other sense derives.

newTerms.definition: A premise is a claim put forward to be accepted on its own grounds; an inference is a claim drawn from earlier claims; the conclusion is the final inference an argument aims to establish. The module's argument steps are labeled with these three kinds.
newTerms.example: “Change occurs” is a premise; “so something actual is actualizing a potential” is an inference drawn from premises.
newTerms.origin: Latin praemissa, “sent before”; inferre, “to bring in”; concludere, “to shut up together.”
newTerms.confuseWith: Assumption: a premise in a demonstration is not merely assumed but defended in the informal discussion.

newTerms.definition: An argument is valid (deductively valid) if its conclusion follows necessarily from its premises; it is sound if it is valid and all its premises are true. A sound argument's conclusion must be true.
newTerms.example: “All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; so Socrates is mortal” is valid, and sound because both premises are true.
newTerms.origin: Standard terms of logic, going back to Aristotle's analysis of deductive reasoning.
newTerms.confuseWith: Persuasiveness: an argument can be valid and sound without convincing everyone, as Feser stresses in answering “no one can claim a proof.”

newTerms.definition: A series that goes back without end, each member depending on a previous one. Feser grants that a linear causal series might regress infinitely, but argues that a hierarchical series cannot consist entirely of members with derived power.
newTerms.example: An infinitely long paintbrush handle still couldn't move itself; the motion must come from something outside the series.
newTerms.origin: Latin regressus, “a going back.”
newTerms.confuseWith: A long but finite series: the argument's point is not about length, since even an infinite series of borrowers would need a lender.

newTerms.definition: The Aristotelian view that physical substances are composites of form (what makes a thing the kind of thing it is, with its distinctive properties) and matter (what individuates the form into this particular thing). Chapter 2 notes that, if the view is true, form and matter are among the parts that require a cause of their combination.
newTerms.example: The form of copper gives any piece of copper its malleability and conductivity; matter makes this piece of copper distinct from that one.
newTerms.origin: Greek hylē, “matter,” plus morphē, “form”; from Aristotle.
newTerms.confuseWith: Shape and stuff in the everyday sense: form in the Aristotelian sense is a thing's nature or organizing principle, not merely its outline.

newTerms.definition: General patterns or features that many individual things can share, such as redness, roundness, triangularity, or humanness. A universal is abstract in that we grasp it by setting aside the individual features of the things that have it.
newTerms.example: Billiard racks, pyramids, and dinner bells all share triangularity; stop signs and strawberries share redness.
newTerms.origin: Latin universalis, “belonging to all”; debated since Plato and Aristotle.
newTerms.confuseWith: A collection of things: triangularity is not the set of all triangles, since it could be exemplified again even if every existing triangle were destroyed.

newTerms.definition: What sentences express: statements about the world that are true or false, distinct from the particular words used to state them. Propositions are counted among abstract objects.
newTerms.example: “Snow is white” and “Schnee ist weiss” are different sentences expressing the same proposition.
newTerms.origin: Latin propositio, “a setting forth.”
newTerms.confuseWith: Sentences: erasing every written sentence stating that snow is white would not make that proposition false or destroy it.

newTerms.definition: Ways things could have been. A possibility in this sense is limited by the laws of logic, not by the laws of physics. Possibilities are among the abstract objects the Augustinian proof says must be grounded in a divine intellect.
newTerms.example: Mars could have had three moons; unicorns could have existed. There is no possible world where 2 + 2 = 5.
newTerms.origin: The phrase is associated with Leibniz and later modal logic.
newTerms.confuseWith: Other physical universes in a multiverse: a possible world is a way things could be, not a place you could travel to.

newTerms.definition: The view, defended in chapter 3, that universals, propositions, and possibilities exist in things and in finite minds but ultimately in an infinite, eternal divine intellect. It agrees with Aristotelian realism (universals exist only in things or in intellects, not in a Platonic third realm) but adds, with Augustine, a divine intellect to ground truths and possibilities no finite thing or mind can.
newTerms.example: The possibility of unicorns, which never existed and was possible before anyone imagined one, is grounded in the divine intellect.
newTerms.origin: Named for the Scholastic tradition; the thesis about divine ideas is associated with Augustine.
newTerms.confuseWith: Platonic realism: Scholastic realism denies any mind-independent third realm and locates abstract objects in an intellect.

newTerms.definition: Two views about universals rejected in chapter 3. Nominalism denies that there are universals and other abstract objects at all, saying there are only general names. Conceptualism grants they are real but holds that they are wholly constructed by the human mind.
newTerms.example: A nominalist says there is the word “red,” but no such thing as redness; a conceptualist says redness is a mental construct.
newTerms.origin: Latin nomen, “name,” and conceptus, “concept”; both views were prominent in late medieval philosophy.
newTerms.confuseWith: Aristotelian realism, which agrees that universals don't exist in a separate realm but insists they really exist in things.

newTerms.definition: God's mind: the divine capacity to know, together with will, the capacity to choose and love. Classical theists attribute intellect and will to God, understood analogically, which is why they regard God as personal. The Augustinian proof concludes to a divine intellect in which abstract objects ultimately exist.
newTerms.example: Just as an architect's concept of a pyramid exists in his mind, all universals and possibilities exist as ideas in God's intellect.
newTerms.origin: Latin intellectus, “understanding,” and voluntas, “will.”
newTerms.confuseWith: A human-like mind with changing thoughts: the divine intellect is not a composite mental apparatus, and God's knowledge is identical with his being.

newTerms.definition: What a thing is: the nature that makes it the kind of thing it is. Essence is contrasted with existence (the fact that the thing is), and in all contingent things the two are really distinct.
newTerms.example: The essence of a human being is traditionally defined as rational animality; knowing it doesn't tell you whether any humans exist.
newTerms.origin: Latin essentia, from esse, “to be”; Aristotle's “what it is to be” a thing.
newTerms.confuseWith: A thing's contingent accidents, such as skin color: those belong to a thing without being part of what it is.

newTerms.definition: A genus is a broader class, a species a narrower class within it, and the specific difference is what distinguishes one species from others in the same genus. God, being simple, falls under no genus.
newTerms.example: Humans belong to the genus animal; rationality is the specific difference that marks them off from other animals.
newTerms.origin: Latin genus, “kind,” species, “appearance” or “kind,” and differentia; from Aristotle's logic (not the narrower sense in modern biology).
newTerms.confuseWith: Biological classification: the logical and metaphysical sense is broader than the technical biological sense.

newTerms.definition: The tradition of Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz, which held that some knowledge comes from reason alone, often through ideas the mind is born with (innate ideas). Feser's rationalist proof shares their commitment to PSR but not their theory of knowledge.
newTerms.example: Descartes held that the idea of God is innate in the human mind.
newTerms.origin: “Continental” because its leading figures worked on the European continent, in contrast to British empiricism.
newTerms.confuseWith: Rationalism in the broad sense of relying on reason rather than faith, which Feser does embrace against fideism.

newTerms.definition: The part of philosophy that studies knowledge: what it is, how we get it, and how beliefs are justified. The introduction says the rationalist proof carries none of the continental rationalists' epistemology.
newTerms.example: Asking whether we can trust our senses, or whether some ideas are innate, is an epistemological question.
newTerms.origin: Greek epistēmē, “knowledge,” plus logos, “study.”
newTerms.confuseWith: Metaphysics, which studies what exists and its nature rather than how we know it.

newTerms.definition: A way of establishing a claim by showing that denying it leads to absurdity or self-contradiction. Feser defends PSR this way, arguing that its denial undermines the reasoning of the person who denies it.
newTerms.example: If PSR were false, our beliefs might have no connection to good reasons — including the belief that PSR is false.
newTerms.origin: Latin, “reduction to the absurd.”
newTerms.confuseWith: Ridicule: a reductio is a logical demonstration that a position implies something impossible, not a mocking dismissal.

newTerms.definition: A fact with no explanation at all. Some critics of PSR hold that the most basic laws of nature, or the universe itself, are brute facts. Feser argues that an explanatory chain ending in a brute fact explains nothing.
newTerms.example: A book held up by a shelf whose own staying up is a brute fact: the shelf has no real tendency to pass on, so the book's position isn't really explained.
newTerms.origin: A term from modern analytic philosophy (used by critics of PSR such as Bertrand Russell in his debate with Copleston).
newTerms.confuseWith: A fact we haven't yet explained: a brute fact is supposed to have no explanation whatsoever, not merely an unknown one.

newTerms.definition: The regularities science describes, such as the law of gravity. Feser argues they cannot be the ultimate explanation of things: laws describe how things with certain natures behave, and a series of ever more fundamental laws is like a hierarchical series that needs a first member.
newTerms.example: Hawking and Mlodinow suggest the universe can create itself because there is a law like gravity; Feser replies that a law is not nothing and cannot explain its own existence.
newTerms.origin: A phrase that became central in early modern science (Descartes, Newton).
newTerms.confuseWith: Causes: a law describes a pattern of behavior and does not by itself make anything happen or exist.

newTerms.definition: A supernatural effect has as its cause something outside the natural order altogether, so only God can produce it. A preternatural effect is extraordinary but still produced by a created being, such as an angel, that belongs to the natural order broadly understood.
newTerms.example: A true miracle, like raising the dead, is supernatural; a merely astonishing feat an angel might perform would be preternatural.
newTerms.origin: Latin supra naturam, “above nature,” and praeter naturam, “beyond (the ordinary course of) nature”; Feser follows Ramelow here.
newTerms.confuseWith: Paranormal in the popular sense: “supernatural” in Feser's account is a precise claim about the cause being God.

newTerms.definition: An argument for God's existence that starts from general features of the world we experience — change, causation, composition, contingency — and reasons to a first or ultimate cause. Four of Feser's five proofs (all but the Augustinian) are cosmological arguments in this broad sense.
newTerms.example: Aquinas' first three Ways, and Feser's Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, Thomistic, and rationalist proofs.
newTerms.origin: Greek kosmos, “world”; the label was popularized by Kant.
newTerms.confuseWith: The ontological argument, which reasons from the concept of God alone rather than from features of the world.

newTerms.definition: A cosmological argument, prominent in medieval Islamic philosophy and revived by William Lane Craig, that reasons from the claim that the universe began to exist to a cause of its beginning. Feser's proofs are not of this type: they don't depend on a beginning.
newTerms.example: “Whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; so the universe has a cause.”
newTerms.origin: From the Arabic kalām, a tradition of dialectical theology.
newTerms.confuseWith: Feser's hierarchical, here-and-now arguments, which grant that the universe might have had no beginning.

newTerms.definition: The scientific model on which the observable universe expanded from an extremely hot, dense early state about 13.8 billion years ago. Feser treats the question of whether it marks an absolute beginning as irrelevant to his proofs.
newTerms.example: Critics ask what caused the Big Bang; Feser replies that even an eternal universe would need a sustaining cause now.
newTerms.origin: Term popularized (originally dismissively) by astronomer Fred Hoyle in 1949.
newTerms.confuseWith: The first cause of Feser's proofs: the Big Bang is at most a first event in time, not a cause with underived power.

newTerms.definition: The hypothesis that our universe is one of many, perhaps branching from earlier universes in a beginningless series. Rosenberg and Krauss invoke it against first-cause arguments; Feser grants it for argument's sake, since a multiverse would still need a sustaining cause.
newTerms.example: “Our Big Bang branched off from a prior universe, and so on forever.”
newTerms.origin: A term from modern cosmology and physics.
newTerms.confuseWith: Possible worlds in philosophy, which are ways things could be, not physically existing universes.

newTerms.definition: Theism is belief that God exists; atheism is the view that God does not exist; agnosticism is the view that we do not or cannot know whether God exists. The introduction claims that if the proofs succeed, the theism–atheism debate is settled and the remaining debate is among theists.
newTerms.example: Jews, Christians, Muslims, Hindus, and purely philosophical theists are all theists in this sense.
newTerms.origin: Greek theos, “god”; a-, “without”; agnōstos, “unknown” (the last term coined by T. H. Huxley).
newTerms.confuseWith: Classical theism, which is one specific conception of the God theists believe in.

newTerms.definition: The Christian teaching that the one God is three persons (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit). Feser's example of a truth knowable only by revelation, not by natural theology.
newTerms.example: Chapter 7 notes that the five proofs don't show that God is a Trinity, and says this is true but irrelevant to their aim.
newTerms.origin: Latin trinitas, “threeness.”
newTerms.confuseWith: A claim of natural theology: on standard Catholic teaching, which Feser cites, the Trinity can be known only through revelation.

newTerms.definition: Assuming, in the premises, the very conclusion an argument is supposed to prove. Feser lists question-begging, alongside false premises and invalid inferences, as a legitimate way to show a demonstration fails.
newTerms.example: Arguing “God exists because the Bible says so, and the Bible is true because God wrote it” begs the question.
newTerms.origin: A translation of the Latin petitio principii, “asking for the starting point.”
newTerms.confuseWith: “Raising the question”: in logic, begging the question means circular reasoning, not prompting a further question.

newTerms.definition: A design-style argument that the physical constants of the universe fall within a narrow range permitting life, which is taken to make a designer probable. It is probabilistic and depends on current science, unlike Feser's proofs.
newTerms.example: “If gravity were slightly stronger, stars couldn't form; this is best explained by design.”
newTerms.origin: A late twentieth-century argument drawing on physics and cosmology.
newTerms.confuseWith: Feser's demonstrations, which don't rest on any particular scientific data.

newTerms.definition: The view that everything that exists is material or physical. Feser uses it as an example of a disputed philosophical position whose arguments are not dismissed merely because they have critics.
newTerms.example: A materialist might claim that the mind is nothing but the brain.
newTerms.origin: From Latin materia, “matter”; traced back to ancient atomists like Democritus.
newTerms.confuseWith: Materialism in the everyday sense of caring about possessions.

newTerms.definition: A modern school of thought associated with Charles Hartshorne (following Whitehead) that holds that God changes and develops along with the world. Feser counts it as a form of theistic personalism, since changeability implies potentiality and composition.
newTerms.example: A process theologian might say God's experience grows richer as the world's history unfolds.
newTerms.origin: Named after Alfred North Whitehead's “philosophy of process” (twentieth century).
newTerms.confuseWith: Classical theism, which holds that God is immutable because he is pure actuality.

newTerms.definition: Apologetics is the reasoned defense of a religious position; a cumulative-case approach combines many probabilistic considerations (design, fine-tuning, religious experience, and so on) to argue that theism is more likely than not. Feser's approach instead aims at demonstration.
newTerms.example: An apologist might argue that fine-tuning plus consciousness plus moral facts together make God the best explanation.
newTerms.origin: Greek apologia, “a speech in defense.”
newTerms.confuseWith: Apologizing: apologetics means defending a view, not saying sorry for it.

newTerms.definition: The ancient argument that change is impossible, since for something to come to be, it would have to come from nothing. Aristotle answered it by distinguishing actuality and potentiality: change is the actualization of a potential, and a potential is not nothing.
newTerms.example: Parmenides would say the coffee's coldness cannot come to be, since before the cooling it was nothing.
newTerms.origin: Parmenides of Elea, Greek philosopher of the fifth century B.C.
newTerms.confuseWith: Modern claims that time is an illusion: Parmenides' argument is a logical argument about being and nothing, not a physical theory.
